This glossary is your foundation. Every term here maps directly to a tactic, a measurement, or a competitive advantage. Read it. Share it. Optimize against it.

## **Section 1: The 12 Core Acronyms & Disciplines Every Marketer Must Know**

These are the foundational terms — the ones that appear in every strategy deck, audit, and client briefing in 2026.

Core

### **GEO — Generative Engine Optimization**

The practice of structuring content and managing online presence to improve visibility in responses generated by AI systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude. GEO focuses on making content the preferred source that generative AI draws upon when answering queries. Originated in a 2023 Princeton/Georgia Tech/IIT Delhi research paper demonstrating 30–40% visibility uplift from optimized content.

**PRO TIP:** GEO is not just about being found — it's about being cited. The goal is AI attribution, not just a ranking.

Core

### AEO — Answer Engine Optimization

Structuring on-page content so an answer engine can extract a clean, standalone passage and serve it as a direct answer. Core tactics include question-led H2s, one-sentence direct replies beneath each heading, short definitional paragraphs, and schema markup. AEO emerged as Google began displaying featured snippets and knowledge panels. GEO and AEO are largely synonymous — AEO focuses on extractable passages, GEO covers the broader generative surface.

Core

### LLMO — Large Language Model Optimization

Also called LLM Optimization. The practice of influencing how large language models understand, recall, and represent your brand — both in training data and in live retrieval. Overlaps heavily with GEO but emphasises entity-level brand presence across the full LLM ecosystem, not just individual citations.

**PRO TIP:** LLMO requires consistent entity signals across Wikipedia, press coverage, and structured data — not just on-page copy.

Core

### AIO — AI Optimization / AI Overviews Optimization

A term with two common meanings. Some marketers use AIO as a catch-all for every AI search tactic. Others use it specifically for optimizing content to appear inside Google's AI Overviews feature. Always verify context before building a strategy around this acronym — it's being used inconsistently across the industry in 2026.

Core

### AI SEO — AI Search Engine Optimization

The umbrella term for any SEO practice aimed at improving visibility across AI-powered search surfaces — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Mode, and beyond. AI SEO encompasses AEO, GEO, LLMO, and AIO as component disciplines rather than replacing them. Think of it as the new category label for "modern search marketing."

Core

### SEO — Search Engine Optimization (Evolved)

The original practice of optimizing content so traditional search engines rank it higher in results. In 2026, some industry voices have reframed SEO to mean "Search Everywhere Optimization" — reflecting visibility across Google, social search platforms, and AI-powered results. The foundational principles of quality, authority, and relevance remain unchanged.

Core

### SXO — Search Experience Optimization

The combination of SEO and UX (User Experience). A technically perfect answer served on a slow, cluttered page still loses — because both users and search engines reward the full experience, not just the textual content. SXO treats on-page engagement metrics as ranking signals in their own right.

Core

### E-E-A-T — Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness

Google's quality framework, extended from E-A-T in 2022 to add "Experience" as the first pillar. All four signals are used by both traditional search algorithms and AI systems to evaluate source credibility. First-hand experience signals have become especially valuable in AI search, as LLMs increasingly distinguish between direct knowledge and second-hand reporting.

**PRO TIP:** The first "E" (Experience) is where most content still under-delivers. Add first-hand data, testing notes, and personal observations.

Core

### RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation

A technical architecture where an AI system first retrieves relevant documents or passages from a search index (retrieval), then uses that retrieved content to inform its generated answer (augmentation). RAG systems cite real sources and are less prone to hallucination than pure generative models. Most AI search products (Perplexity, ChatGPT Search, Google AI Mode) use RAG-based architectures.

Core

### SGE — Search Generative Experience

Google's original brand name for its AI-generated answer feature, piloted through 2023–2024. Now replaced in the product by the "AI Overviews" and "AI Mode" branding. SGE is still referenced in older articles and research, so understanding it is important for context — especially when reviewing case studies or studies from the 2023–2024 period.

Core

### NLP — Natural Language Processing

The branch of AI that enables machines to understand, interpret, and generate human language. NLP is the foundational technology behind all modern search engines and large language models. Understanding NLP principles helps explain why semantic content, entity optimization, and natural writing styles outperform keyword-stuffed content in AI-era search.

Core

### LLM — Large Language Model

A text-based AI model trained on vast quantities of text data that predicts the next most probable token (word fragment) based on patterns in that training and the context it currently sees. ChatGPT (GPT-4o), Claude, Gemini, and Llama are all LLMs. Understanding LLMs is foundational to every GEO and AEO strategy — they are the engines you are optimizing for.

## Section 2: The 10 AI Platforms & Models You Need to Optimize For

These are the platforms where your content either gets cited — or gets invisible. Know each one's citation behavior and ranking signals.

### The AI Search Ecosystem in 2026

The major platforms where content visibility is won or lost

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201920%20788'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Platform

### ChatGPT Search

OpenAI's search-integrated mode that fetches live web content via Microsoft Bing (and increasingly Google's index) to supplement training data with current information. Processes approximately 2.5 billion prompts daily, of which 65% qualify as search. Has a 96% lower click-through rate than Google — meaning citations here rarely generate direct traffic, but build brand authority and influence purchasing decisions invisibly.

Platform

### Google AI Overviews

Google's AI-generated answer box powered by Gemini, appearing above traditional search results for a rapidly growing share of queries — expanding from 6.49% of queries in January 2025 to over 25% by mid-2025. The single most impactful platform for brands with existing Google SEO authority, as AI Overviews draw heavily from pages already ranking in the top 10. Reduces organic CTR by an average of 58% for queries where it appears.

**PRO TIP:** Pages already ranking #1–#5 are most likely to be cited in AI Overviews. Strong traditional SEO still feeds GEO here.

Platform

### Google AI Mode

A dedicated AI-first search experience launched at Google I/O 2025, handling complex multi-part queries through "fan-out search" — breaking a single prompt into hundreds of parallel sub-queries and synthesizing the results. AI Mode is distinct from AI Overviews: it replaces the traditional SERP entirely for complex queries, making citation here especially valuable.

Platform

### Perplexity

An AI-native answer engine built around citation-first responses, showing users attributed source links for every claim. Serves 780+ million monthly queries. Perplexity's citation behavior is unusually transparent — making it a primary benchmark platform for AEO/GEO measurement. Notable for its "Perplexity Pages" feature, which generates AI-authored topic pages that frequently cite high-authority sources.

Platform

### Claude (Anthropic)

Anthropic's conversational AI product line. Particularly valued in enterprise and developer contexts for its long-context reasoning capabilities and commitment to accuracy. Claude with Web Search extends its knowledge beyond training data through live retrieval and citation. Claude reportedly places particular emphasis on epistemic precision — content that qualifies claims accurately is more likely to be cited.

Platform

### Gemini / Gemini Advanced

Google's family of large language models powering Google AI Mode, AI Overviews, and the standalone Gemini app. Gemini Advanced is the premium tier with enhanced multi-modal reasoning. Because Gemini drives both AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, optimizing for Gemini has the broadest reach of any single AI platform optimisation effort.

Platform

### Microsoft Copilot

Microsoft's AI assistant built on OpenAI's GPT models and powered by Bing's search index. Integrated into Windows, Edge, and Microsoft 365. Copilot is important for B2B marketers in particular — it operates within the Microsoft ecosystem where many corporate users conduct their research, and its search grounding relies on Bing's index rather than Google's.

Platform

### Generative AI (Definition)

AI systems that produce new content — text, images, audio, code, video — based on patterns learned from training data. The parent category that contains LLMs. Generative AI is the broad technological shift driving the entire GEO discipline. Understanding that these systems generate novel responses (not retrieve pre-written ones) is key to understanding why content strategy must change.

Platform

### AI Agents

AI systems that take multi-step autonomous actions — not just answering questions, but browsing, filling forms, calling APIs, and chaining tasks. OpenAI Operator, Anthropic's Claude computer use, and Google's Project Mariner are early-stage examples. AI agents represent the next frontier of GEO: as agents make purchasing decisions, recommend services, and conduct research autonomously, brand presence in AI memory becomes a direct commercial asset.

**PRO TIP:** 2026 is the year to double down on AI agent visibility — brands cited by agents in research mode will have first-mover advantage.

Platform

### Voice Search / Smart Speakers

Search queries delivered verbally via Siri, Google Assistant, Alexa, or smart home devices. Voice search was the original "answer engine" use case that drove early AEO strategy. In 2026, voice and AI text search are converging — the same structured, direct-answer content formats that win AI citations also win voice search responses. Mobile-first, conversational content serves both.

## Section 3: 11 Technical GEO Infrastructure Terms

The back-end mechanics that determine whether AI systems can access, understand, and cite your content.

Technical

### Schema Markup / Structured Data

Machine-readable labels embedded in your HTML that tell search engines and AI systems exactly what each piece of content represents — an FAQ entry, a product, a review, an author biography, a how-to step. Schema markup (implemented via JSON-LD) significantly improves AI systems' ability to extract accurate, citable information from your pages. FAQ schema is one of the highest-impact single technical changes for AEO.

**PRO TIP:** Implement FAQ, Article, HowTo, and Organization schema as a minimum baseline for any GEO-ready site.

Technical

### LLMs.txt

A proposed Markdown file served at /llms.txt that provides AI crawlers with a curated sitemap of your most important pages, complete with brief descriptions. Analogous to robots.txt for traditional bots but optimized for AI understanding. Helps direct limited AI crawl budget toward your most authoritative content. Adoption is growing but impact remains debated — treat it as low-cost hygiene with upside potential.

Technical

### SSR — Server-Side Rendering

Returning fully rendered HTML from the server rather than relying on JavaScript to populate content in the browser. Most AI crawlers cannot execute JavaScript — meaning that content rendered client-side (via React, Vue, Angular SPA frameworks) may be completely invisible to AI systems. SSR is effectively required for reliable AI indexation and is the single most impactful technical fix for JavaScript-heavy websites targeting GEO visibility.

Technical

### Chunking

The practice of breaking a page into self-contained sections — each answering one discrete question or covering one specific sub-topic — with clear headings. Strong chunking helps retrieval systems identify and extract the precise passage relevant to a query, rather than pulling in surrounding context that adds noise. Well-chunked content has significantly higher citation probability in RAG-based AI systems.

Technical

### Passage Indexing

An AI system's ability to identify and cite specific passages within a long document, rather than attributing the document as a whole. Google introduced passage indexing for traditional search in 2021; it's now standard in AI retrieval. Clear H2 and H3 heading structure, with one topic per section, is the primary enabler of accurate passage-level citation.

Technical

### Entity Recognition

The AI's ability to identify and understand named entities — people, organizations, products, locations, concepts — within your content. Strong entity optimisation through consistent naming conventions, schema markup, and cross-platform presence (Wikipedia, Wikidata, Google Knowledge Graph) helps AI systems accurately understand who and what your content is about, increasing the likelihood of accurate attribution.

Technical

### Knowledge Graph

A structured database of entities and relationships that helps AI systems understand connections between people, brands, topics, and concepts. Google's Knowledge Graph powers Knowledge Panels and informs AI Overviews. Having your brand, key personnel, and products represented in knowledge graphs is a foundational LLMO strategy — it shapes how AI systems "understand" your brand, independent of any individual piece of content.

Technical

### Token Efficiency

In AI content processing, the ability to convey maximum information in minimum tokens (word fragments). AI systems have finite context windows — they cannot process unlimited text. Well-structured, concise content that delivers its key claims in the fewest possible tokens is more likely to be fully processed and cited accurately. Avoid filler phrasing, excessive preambles, and bloated introductions.

Technical

### Inference-Time Retrieval

The process by which a RAG-based AI system fetches live web content at the moment of answering a query (inference time), rather than relying solely on training data. This is how ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode provide current information. Content optimized for inference-time retrieval needs to be fast-loading, structured, and consistently published/updated to be crawlable when queries arise.

Technical

### Crawl Budget (AI)

The extent to which an AI crawler will index your site during any given period. Unlike Google, which maintains comprehensive crawl budgets for established sites, AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot) are often more selective. LLMs.txt, clear internal linking, fast page speeds, and clean XML sitemaps all help ensure AI crawlers prioritize your most authoritative content over thin or duplicate pages.

Technical

### Programmatic SEO

The practice of generating large numbers of templated pages from a database to target long-tail queries at scale. Still viable in 2026 when the output is genuinely useful and unique — but increasingly risky when pages are thin or near-duplicate, as AI systems apply quality filters that devalue low-value programmatic content. High-quality programmatic pages (with original data, genuine depth) can be powerful citation targets for specific query clusters.

## Section 4: 9 Content Strategy & Format Terms for AI Visibility

How you structure, format, and present content determines whether AI systems can find, extract, and cite it.

Content

### Citation Anchor

A highly specific, quotable fact or insight within a piece of content that AI engines consistently extract and cite across multiple platforms. Original statistics, named methodologies, unique frameworks, and proprietary data points serve as citation anchors. Once established, citation anchors generate ongoing AI visibility independently of new content production — they become durable authority assets.

**PRO TIP:** Commission original research. A single proprietary statistic can become a citation anchor across hundreds of AI responses.

Content

### Answer Density

The ratio of direct, quotable answers to total word count in a piece of content. High-answer-density pages deliver their key claims early and concisely, without extensive padding or keyword-stuffing. AI systems reward answer density because they are optimizing for the user's question, not your SEO metrics. Aim for the shortest path from question to answer — then add depth for human readers.

Content

### Q&A Structuring

Formatting pages as explicit question-answer pairs, with the question as the H2 or H3 heading and the direct answer as the first sentence (or short paragraph) directly beneath it. Q&A structuring is the single most impactful content format change for AEO and AI citation probability. Questions should precisely match how users phrase queries — use "People Also Ask" data and conversational query research to source them.

Content

### Topical Authority

The breadth and depth of coverage your website has on a given subject, as perceived by search engines and AI systems. Sites that cover a topic comprehensively — from introductory definitions through to advanced, specific questions — signal genuine expertise. Topical authority is built through topic clustering: a pillar page (broad overview) supported by multiple cluster pages (specific sub-topics), all internally linked.

Content

### Semantic Coherence

The degree to which all elements of a page consistently address the same core topic without unrelated tangents. GEO rewards focused, semantically coherent content over sprawling keyword-targeting pages that try to rank for unrelated queries through volume. Each page should have one clear topical purpose, answerable in a single sentence.

Content

### Answer Graph

An internally linked content ecosystem that covers a topic comprehensively from multiple angles: definition pages, comparison pages, how-to guides, FAQ clusters, and case studies — all linked together. An answer graph ensures that for any AI query related to your topic area, there is a highly relevant, deeply authoritative page on your site that serves as the ideal citation source.

Content

### Direct Answer / AI Snippet

A short extract that an AI engine quotes directly inside its generated response. Writing self-contained sentences that answer a specific question in isolation (e.g., "GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization, the practice of...") makes content snippet-ready. Direct answers should be formulated to function as standalone sentences — they will often be cited without surrounding context.

Content

### Epistemic Precision

The degree to which content makes accurately qualified claims with appropriate certainty levels. Saying "studies suggest X in approximately Y% of cases" is more epistemically precise than "X always happens." AI systems — particularly Claude — reward epistemic precision, as it signals rigorous, trustworthy sourcing. Overconfident, unsupported claims reduce citation probability and E-E-A-T signals simultaneously.

Content

### Listicle / Enumerated Content

List-based content with numbered or bulleted items. AI engines extract listicles cleanly because each item has an unambiguous start and end point, making them ideal passage indexing targets. "Top 5 reasons," "7 ways to," and "The 3 main types of" formats consistently outperform prose-only content for AI citation rates, particularly for informational and comparison queries.

**PRO TIP:** Use numbered lists wherever possible — ordinal structure ("3 steps to") signals completeness to AI synthesis engines.

## Section 5: 8 Measurement & Performance Terms for GEO ROI

If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. These are the metrics that actually matter for AI search performance.

Measurement

### GEO Visibility Score

A composite metric representing how often and how prominently your brand appears across AI engine answers for a defined set of target queries. Typically calculated by sampling a representative query set across multiple AI platforms (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude), measuring citation rate, position prominence, and sentiment of each mention. The GEO equivalent of organic search ranking position.

Measurement

### Share of Voice (AI)

Your brand's proportional presence in AI-generated answers for a defined topic area, expressed as a percentage of total mentions across a set of queries. "If someone asks an AI anything about \[your industry\], what % of the time is your brand mentioned?" Share of voice is the strategic metric that GEO optimisation ultimately moves — and the one most closely correlated with AI-influenced purchasing decisions.

**PRO TIP:** Track share of voice across all major AI platforms separately — citation patterns vary significantly by platform.

Measurement

### Citation Rate

The percentage of times your domain is cited as a source across a set of AI-generated responses for target queries. Citation rate is the most direct GEO performance metric. Unlike traditional rankings (binary in/out), citation rate is probabilistic — the same query may return your domain 6 out of 10 times due to AI non-determinism. Measurement requires multiple runs per query.

Measurement

### Competitive Citation Gap

The difference between your citation rate and a competitor's on the same set of target queries. The competitive citation gap is the primary strategic target for GEO — identifying which specific queries your competitors win and you don't, and closing that gap through content improvement, authority building, and structured data. A negative gap means you're losing AI mindshare to competitors.

Measurement

### AI Traffic

Website visits that originate from clicks within AI-generated answers. Currently a small but rapidly growing percentage of total traffic for most sites — but this metric understates the actual impact of AI visibility, since most AI answers are consumed without a click. AI traffic should be tracked separately in analytics (via referrer data from ChatGPT, Perplexity, etc.) and reported alongside share of voice metrics.

Measurement

### Non-Determinism (AI)

The property that identical prompts submitted to an AI system can produce different outputs — including different source citations — each time. Non-determinism means that AI citation tracking requires statistical sampling across many runs, not a single test. A citation rate of 70% means your content was cited 7 out of 10 times on that query — not that it always or never appears.

Measurement

### Zero-Click Rate

The proportion of searches that end without the user clicking through to any external website, because their query was answered directly on the SERP or in the AI response. Zero-click rates on AI-heavy queries dramatically exceed those on traditional search. This means traditional traffic metrics will undercount AI-influenced brand awareness — marketers need to supplement click-based analytics with survey-based brand attribution studies.

Measurement

### AI Brand Sentiment

The tone and framing with which AI systems describe your brand when mentioning it in responses. AI systems don't just cite brands — they contextualise them. Appearing as "a leading provider of X" carries very different brand value than "X company, which has faced criticism for Y." Monitoring AI brand sentiment across platforms is an emerging reputation management discipline closely related to GEO.

## Section 6: 9 Query, Intent & Retrieval Terms

How users talk to AI — and how AI retrieves answers. Understanding the query layer is essential for content targeting.

Query

### Conversational Query

A search request phrased in natural, full-sentence language rather than keyword fragments. "What are the best B2B SaaS marketing strategies for a Series A startup?" rather than "B2B SaaS marketing." AI-era queries average 20+ words. Content optimized for conversational queries uses natural language, addresses context, and anticipates follow-up questions.

Query

### Multi-Turn Conversation

An AI search interaction involving multiple sequential follow-up questions, allowing users to refine and deepen a line of inquiry within a single session. Multi-turn conversations mean that being cited in the first response dramatically increases the likelihood of being cited in subsequent responses in the same session. Comprehensive content that anticipates follow-up questions captures this reinforcement effect.

**PRO TIP:** Build "conversation-ready" content that answers the likely next 2–3 questions after your primary answer.

Query

### Fan-Out Queries

When an AI system breaks a single user prompt into multiple related sub-queries, runs them in parallel, and synthesizes the combined results. Google Deep Search (within AI Mode) can generate hundreds of sub-queries for a single complex question. Fan-out architecture means that topically comprehensive content — covering many related sub-questions on one page — has a higher probability of being retrieved for at least one of the sub-queries.

Query

### Informational Query

A query seeking factual knowledge or explanation: "What is GEO?", "How does Perplexity work?", "What are the benefits of structured data?" Informational queries are the dominant use case for AI search — they represent the highest volume opportunity for GEO citation. Definitions, explanations, comparisons, and how-to content are the content formats that win informational queries.

Query

### Transactional Query (AI)

A query with commercial purchase intent — "best GEO agency in London," "GEO services pricing," "compare GEO platforms." Transactional queries are increasingly being handled by AI systems in 2026, with product recommendations and service comparisons appearing in AI Overviews and ChatGPT responses. Optimizing category and product pages for AI citation on transactional queries is a direct revenue-generation GEO tactic.

Query

### Search Grounding

Forcing an LLM to retrieve live web evidence before generating its answer, rather than relying solely on training data. Search grounding reduces AI hallucination and ties responses to verifiable, citable sources. From a GEO perspective, well-grounded AI systems are more likely to cite accurately — but also more competitive, as only genuinely authoritative content survives the grounding retrieval step.

Query

### Semantic Search

Search that matches conceptual meaning and user intent rather than exact keyword strings. As search and AI converge, semantic understanding has become the baseline expectation. A page about "GEO" can now rank for "how to appear in AI answers," "AI search optimisation," and "generative engine visibility" — without containing those exact phrases — if its semantic content is strong and contextually rich.

Query

### Featured Snippet

The extracted answer Google highlights at the top of traditional search results, above all organic rankings. Often the first piece of content AI Overviews reference when forming their answers for navigational and informational queries where Google has strong traditional ranking signals. Winning featured snippets on your target queries remains one of the strongest predictors of AI Overviews citation.

Query

### SERP (AI Era Definition)

Search Engine Results Page. In 2026, a Google SERP for many queries blends: AI Overviews (top), Featured Snippets, People Also Ask boxes, traditional organic results, and rich results (maps, reviews, products) — sometimes with AI Mode accessible as a separate tab. Understanding the modern SERP composition helps prioritize which GEO tactics drive the most visible results for your target queries.

## Section 7: 7 UX & Quality Signal Terms

The page-level and site-level signals that tell AI systems your content is authoritative, trustworthy, and worth citing.

Quality

### Answer Fidelity

How accurately a piece of content answers a specific question — without off-topic padding, misleading framing, or critical omissions. High answer fidelity is the core content quality signal for GEO. AI systems select sources that best match the user's actual informational need, not sources that merely contain related keywords. Write to answer the question fully and precisely, then stop.

Quality

### Corroboration

Agreement between your content's claims and what other authoritative sources state. Generative AI systems cross-reference multiple sources for consistency before citing any individual one — claims that align with established consensus are significantly more likely to be included in synthesized answers. Disagreeing with expert consensus without strong evidence reduces citation probability regardless of content quality.

Quality

### First-Hand Experience Signal

Content demonstrating that the author personally experienced, tested, used, or investigated the subject being described. The "E" (Experience) in E-E-A-T. AI engines increasingly distinguish between first-hand and second-hand knowledge — content written by practitioners with direct experience consistently outperforms content aggregated from other sources. Case studies, original data, and practitioner observations are high-value experience signals.

**PRO TIP:** Include author bylines with credentials, client results, and original data wherever possible. AI systems attribute credibility at the entity level.

Quality

### Specificity

The level of concrete, quantified detail in a piece of content. GEO rewards specificity: "37% of enterprise marketers increased AI search budget in Q1 2026" is more citable than "many marketers are investing in AI search." Specific data is verifiable, quotable, and trusted by AI synthesis systems — vague generalisations are filtered out in competitive query environments.

Quality

### Topical Completeness

How comprehensively a piece of content covers all relevant dimensions of a topic. AI engines favour sources that provide complete answers over sources addressing only one facet of a multi-part question. For complex queries ("how to build a GEO strategy for an e-commerce brand"), a comprehensive page that addresses research, content architecture, technical setup, and measurement will consistently outperform narrow pages covering only one element.

Quality

### Core Web Vitals

Google's three user experience metrics: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP — loading speed), Interaction to Next Paint (INP — interactivity), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS — visual stability). Core Web Vitals are direct Google ranking signals and indirectly affect GEO — pages with poor CWVs are crawled less frequently, may rank lower in traditional search (reducing AI Overviews citation probability), and create poor experiences that undermine E-E-A-T signals.

Quality

### Earned Media

Third-party coverage, press mentions, citations, and references to your brand across independent publications — not owned or paid. Research from GEO studies (including the University of Toronto 2025 paper) demonstrates that AI search systems show a systematic bias towards earned media over brand-owned content. Press mentions, academic citations, industry directory listings, and journalist quotes all function as "AI authority signals" in ways that traditional SEO has not previously prioritized.

**PRO TIP:** Your PR strategy is now your GEO strategy. Third-party coverage is the highest-value input for LLM citation authority.

## Section 8: 5 Strategic GEO Terms

The higher-level strategic concepts that frame how GEO programmes are built, managed, and scaled.

Strategy

### GEO Audit

A structured assessment of a brand's current visibility across AI search platforms — measuring citation rates, share of voice, content gaps, technical barriers, and competitive positioning. A GEO audit benchmarks where you stand today and identifies the highest-priority improvements for maximum citation uplift. GO MO Group's GEO audit framework is purpose-built for B2B organizations, covering all major AI platforms and delivering a prioritized action roadmap tailored to your industry and buyer journey.

**PRO TIP:** A GEO audit is the essential first step. You cannot optimize what you have not measured.

Strategy

### Content Gap Analysis (AI)

The process of identifying which queries in your target topic area your content does not currently address — creating gaps that competitors fill in AI-generated responses. AI content gap analysis differs from traditional keyword gap analysis: you are identifying questions AI systems are asked that your brand has no citable answer to, rather than keywords your pages don't rank for. Prioritise gaps in high-commercial-intent query clusters first.

Strategy

### Entity Optimization

The practice of ensuring that your brand, products, key personnel, and topics are accurately and consistently represented as named entities across the web — in Wikipedia, Wikidata, Google Business Profile, industry directories, and authoritative external references. Entity optimization shapes how AI systems "understand" your brand independently of any specific page, making it a foundational LLMO strategy that supports all GEO and AEO efforts.

Strategy

### Big Brand Bias

The documented tendency of AI search systems to disproportionately cite large, established brands over smaller or newer entrants — even when smaller brand content is more accurate, recent, or directly relevant. Identified in GEO research as a systemic challenge for challenger brands. Counterstrategies include targeting specific niche query clusters where brand authority is less of a differentiator, and aggressively building earned media signals that signal authority within a specific domain.

Strategy

### AI-First Content Strategy

A content planning and production approach where AI citation potential — not keyword rankings — is the primary optimisation objective. AI-first content is structured around question clusters, features direct answers at the head of each section, incorporates original data as citation anchors, uses schema markup systematically, and measures success through share of voice metrics rather than rank position. Represents the evolution of "content marketing" for the AI search era.

## Section 9: The 4 Major AI Crawlers & What They Index

These are the bots crawling your site for AI training and real-time retrieval. Know each one — and check your robots.txt isn't blocking them.

**GPTBot** OpenAI

Crawls web content for ChatGPT training data and ChatGPT Search retrieval. Block via robots.txt with "User-agent: GPTBot" if you don't want OpenAI to use your content. Allowing access increases ChatGPT citation potential.

**ClaudeBot**

Anthropic

Anthropic's crawler for Claude training and retrieval. Crawls content to build Claude's understanding of web sources. Selectively indexes based on content quality signals. Controllable via robots.txt.

**PerplexityBot**

Perplexity AI

Powers Perplexity's real-time citation engine. Because Perplexity's citation behavior is transparent and trackable, PerplexityBot crawl access is particularly valuable for GEO visibility measurement and citation building.

**Google-Extended**

Google

Google's dedicated crawler for Gemini training and AI Overviews retrieval, separate from Googlebot. Can be blocked independently via robots.txt if you want Google's traditional search to index you but not use your content for AI training.

> **Critical Robots.txt Audit Required**
>
> Check your robots.txt immediately. Many sites have blanket bot-blocking rules — often inherited from generic templates or over-cautious legacy settings — that are blocking all AI crawlers and silently eliminating GEO visibility. If GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, and Google-Extended are blocked, you are invisible to AI search. This is the single most common "quick win" in a GO MO GEO audit.

Quick Reference: SEO vs AEO vs GEO — The Definitive Comparison

### How the 3 Disciplines Differ Across 10 Key Dimensions

| Dimension | Traditional SEO | AEO (Answer Engine Opt.) | GEO (Generative Engine Opt.) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Primary Goal | Rank #1 in Google organic results | Be the direct answer in search | Be cited by AI in generated responses |
| Key Metric | Keyword ranking position | Featured snippet / voice answer wins | Citation rate & share of voice (AI) |
| Content Format | Long-form, keyword-rich pages | Q&A structure, direct answers | Answer-first, chunked, schema-marked |
| Technical Priority | Page speed, mobile, site structure | Schema markup, featured snippet eligibility | SSR, structured data, LLMs.txt, crawl access |
| Authority Signals | Backlinks, domain authority | E-E-A-T, topical authority | Earned media, entity recognition, knowledge graph |
| Traffic Model | Click-through to website | Partial — zero-click risk growing | Largely zero-click; brand influence model |
| Measurement Tools | Google Search Console, Ahrefs, SEMrush | SERP feature trackers, voice analytics | GEO visibility platforms, manual AI sampling |
| JavaScript Sites | Partial — Google renders JS | Partial — JS snippets may not render | Critical Risk — most AI bots can't render JS |
| Original Data Value | Medium — helps link building | Medium — improves credibility | Very High — key citation anchor mechanism |
| PR & Earned Media | Indirect — backlink value | Moderate — E-E-A-T signal | Critical — primary AI authority signal |

# Google Has Published Its Official AI Search Optimisation Guide. Here’s What It Actually Says.

For the first time, Google has released a dedicated resource on optimising content for its generative AI features, including AI Overviews and AI Mode. We've read every line, so you can spend your time acting on it. Below you'll find the plain-English breakdown, the myths Google has put to rest, and what it all means for your strategy.

![](https://www.gomogroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/google-ai-search-optimization.webp)

## **The short version**

Google has published its first official guide to appearing in generative AI features on Search, and the news is encouraging. **Good SEO is still the foundation.** Create genuinely useful, original content, keep your technical house in order, and feel free to ignore most of the "AI SEO hacks" doing the rounds online. In Google's own words, GEO is still SEO. If you've been investing in quality, you're already on the right path.

## **Why this guide matters**

Google's generative AI features, AI Overviews and AI Mode, have changed how millions of people search. Until now, though, official guidance for site owners who want to appear in them has been thin on the ground.

In May 2026, Google Search Central published [a dedicated optimisation guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) alongside the SEO Starter Guide in its core documentation. That placement says a lot. Optimising for generative AI search is now a first-class priority for web publishers, not a niche technical side project.

The guide covers three areas: which foundational SEO practices carry over, what you don't need to do, and how to think about the emerging "agentic" AI experiences. Here's our breakdown.

RAG

The technique Google uses to ground AI answers. It pulls from the core Search index, not from a separate AI database.

AIO

AI Overviews. The AI-generated summaries shown above traditional results for many queries.

GEO

Generative Engine Optimisation. What Google calls “still SEO”, with a renewed focus on content quality and structure.

## **SEO is still the foundation, and Google says so clearly**

The guide opens with a direct answer: yes, SEO still matters for generative AI search. There's no hedging. Google explains that AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on the same ranking and quality systems that power traditional Search.

The mechanism behind this is called **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**. Instead of writing answers from scratch, the AI retrieves relevant, indexed web pages and builds its response from them. For your content to be considered, it needs to be in the index and meet Google's quality signals. The work you've already put into your site counts.

> _"From Google Search's perspective, optimising for generative AI search is optimising for the search experience, and thus still SEO."_
>
> **Google Search Central, May 2026**

Google also describes a second mechanism, **query fan-out**. Here the AI model generates several related sub-queries to build a complete answer. A user asking "how to fix a lawn full of weeds" might trigger sub-queries about herbicides, chemical-free removal and weed prevention. Pages that cover specific, well-defined topics clearly have a better chance of being picked up by those sub-queries.

## **What you should actually do**

### **1\. Create genuinely original content**

This is Google's main message, and it plays to the strengths of anyone with real expertise. The guide separates **commodity content** (common knowledge that's easy to produce with AI and adds no unique insight) from **non-commodity content** (expert or experienced perspectives that go beyond what's available elsewhere).

Google's example makes the point well. "7 Tips for First-Time Homebuyers" is commodity. "Why We Waived the Inspection and Saved Money: A Look Inside the Sewer Line" is not. The second piece comes from lived experience, offers a distinct point of view and is hard to copy. That's exactly the kind of content AI systems are built to surface, and exactly the kind your organisation is able to create.

01

Provide a unique point of viewFirst-hand reviews, original research and expert analysis. Content that only you can produce.

02

Write for human readers firstParagraphs, sections and clear headings. The structure people enjoy reading is the same structure AI can parse.

03

Support text with high-quality images and videoAI Overviews can include visual content. If you already follow image and video SEO best practice, you're optimising for this too.

04

Focus on your visitors' satisfactionGoogle's systems are designed to connect people with content that satisfies them. If you'd be proud to show a visitor your page, you're on the right track.

### **2\. Keep your technical foundation solid**

To appear in generative AI features, a page must be indexed and eligible to appear in Google Search with a snippet. That's the starting point. From there, Google repeats its standard technical guidance: crawlability, clean JavaScript handling, good page experience and less duplicate content.

One detail worth knowing: Google says you don't need perfectly semantic HTML, but semantic markup is still a smart choice. It helps screen readers and accessibility tools, and it makes your pages easier for the new generation of AI agents to navigate (more on that below).

### **3\. Use Merchant Center and Google Business Profile where relevant**

For e-commerce and local businesses, Google's generative AI answers can surface product listings and business information. Merchant Center feeds and Google Business Profiles put that data directly in front of the systems generating those answers. If you haven't set these up yet, it's one of the quickest wins available.

## **What you can stop worrying about**

This may be the most useful part of the guide. Google directly addresses the most common "GEO hacks" being promoted across the industry and confirms that you can leave them off your list:

✕

LLMS.txt files and special AI markupYou don't need to create llms.txt or any other machine-readable AI files. Google may index many file types, but none of them get special treatment in AI features.

✕

"Chunking" content into small piecesGoogle's systems understand multiple topics on a single page. There's no ideal page length, and splitting content into fragments for AI isn't required or particularly helpful.

✕

Rewriting content specifically for AI systemsAI understands synonyms and overall meaning. You don't need to add long-tail keyword variations or rewrite pages to match every possible phrasing of a query.

✕

Seeking inauthentic "mentions" across the webManufactured coverage in forums, blogs or third-party sites doesn't reliably influence AI answers, and it risks breaching spam policies.

✕

Over-investing in structured data for AIStructured data isn't required for generative AI features, and there's no special schema to add. It's still valuable for rich results, but it isn't a lever for AI visibility.

### **GO MO perspective: The fundamentals are your competitive advantage.**

Much of what's sold online as "AEO" or "GEO strategy" relies on tactics Google has now explicitly ruled out. That's good news for anyone who prefers doing things properly. The opportunity isn't in finding new tricks. It's in doing the fundamentals better than competitors who are busy chasing shortcuts. Original expertise, clean architecture and genuine helpfulness: that's the playbook, and it's one you can own.

## **The agentic frontier**

The most forward-looking section of the guide covers AI agents. These are autonomous systems that browse the web on a user's behalf to complete tasks such as booking a table, comparing products or gathering research. Google describes browser agents that analyse screenshots, inspect DOM structure and navigate using accessibility trees.

Google's advice here is measured. This is still emerging, and you only need to engage with it "if it's relevant to your business and you have extra time." The direction is clear, though. Websites that are well-structured, accessible and semantically clean will be easier for these agents to work with, which gives early movers a real head start.

New protocols such as the **Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)** are emerging to standardise how agents transact with websites. This space will grow in importance, especially for e-commerce and service businesses.

## **What this means for B2B marketers**

Google's guide is written for a broad audience, but the implications for B2B deserve their own spotlight.

**Content depth matters more than content volume.** B2B buyers ask complex, specific questions that commodity content can't answer. One well-researched article built on internal data, client experience or genuine technical knowledge is worth more, for AI citations and for conversions, than a library of generic posts. Your expertise is the asset.

**Technical buyers are increasingly AI-mediated.** Someone researching industrial equipment, SaaS platforms or professional services is now likely to see an AI Overview before a traditional result. Earning a citation there takes exactly what the guide describes: authoritative, original, well-structured content.

**The "AI SEO agency" market is full of noise.** Now that Google has said clearly that llms.txt files, content chunking and manufactured mentions don't work, B2B marketing leaders can confidently question any vendor leading with them as differentiators.

### **The practical checklist**

Is your content indexed and snippet-eligible? Is it genuinely original, built on expertise or experience your competitors don't have? Is the page technically clean, crawlable and accessible? Are you using Google Business Profile or Merchant Center where relevant? **If you can answer yes to all four, you're well positioned for generative AI search.** Everything else is secondary.

# Prepare for the next big update to search: MUM

Google has already started rolling out its next major update to Search. Announced in spring 2021, with basic features of the update rolling out the same year, MUM (Multimodal Unified Model) is a huge leap in the search engine’s ability to interpret and contextualize search queries.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%202240%201260'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Adapting Your Digital Marketing to MUM

MUM is the latest update in Google’s developments of their search engine. It represents another leap in identifying presenting the most relevant and trustworthy web results for each search query.

As search engines become increasingly proficient at identifying the best web pages to show their users, businesses must keep their [SEO strategies](https://www.gomogroup.com/en/services/seo-search-engine-optimization/) updated to ensure a great user experience on their digital marketing channels and use data to optimize their communications. This is part of a long trend of smarter search engines and [the importance of Pull Marketing](https://www.gomogroup.com/insikter/paradigm-shift-in-digital-marketing/). In appealing to end-users and search engines alike, relevance and user experience are the most important SEO factors.

The next iteration of Google Search means that companies must consider their target audience in all parts of their website, and ensure that all content is optimized instead of focusing on some “core” elements.

The technology runs on the latest findings in AI language processing and is reportedly 1,000 times more powerful than [BERT](https://blog.google/products/search/search-language-understanding-bert/), the previous installment. In short, researchers used combinations of learning methods to find the optimal way to train a language processing framework, then training it on a colossal dataset. If you’re interested in the nitty-gritty technical details, a [Google blog](https://ai.googleblog.com/2020/02/exploring-transfer-learning-with-t5.html) goes into the details and showcases some of the things the AI can do.

## A Deeper Understanding of Context and Topics

Being armed with an unprecedented understanding of language, MUM will be able to take Google’s interpretation of user intent and the context of results further than before. The first step of MUM’s rollout has been to “zoom” in and out from a topic. This is seen in the suggestions to refine or broaden a search, where the search engine shows results based on the topic, rather than any keywords.

![Improve Search Methods | GO MO Group](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20700%20700'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

This contextual understanding also allows the search engine to process more complex queries. Whereas some complex questions can take eight “manual” searches, MUM could mean that users get all the relevant information from a single query. This means that your content that covers one aspect of a query could still be presented among the results even if not directly related to any of the words used in the search.

#### How should businesses adapt?

This is not a completely new phenomenon, but rather a continuation of a previous trend. The previous big update, BERT, gave the search engine a basic understanding of intent, rather than being bound to the specific words used in search queries.

The improved understanding of topics and context means that businesses should focus even more on covering a wide range of topics in their content marketing strategy. This means that a content strategy should answer both broad, top-level queries as well as many different specific questions.

As specific keywords become less relevant, other factors of SEO play a larger role. Softer qualities, such as content usefulness and user experience, are becoming more important as Google Search finds new ways to measure these. [Search engine optimized web development](https://www.gomogroup.com/en/services/web-development-and-design/) has never been more important as UX factors have more “weight” in ranking.

The deeper understanding of topics also allows Google to use data from sources in different languages to serve relevant information to searchers. Decision-makers looking for suppliers in their native language could now be shown information from a global actor with an English site, and find the website that way. This would mean that a high E-A-T score means increased visibility and relevance for a completely new set of users. Multilingual web pages could see improved synergies between the different versions of pages.

## Adapting to Multimodal Search Queries

Perhaps the biggest update in MUM is the _multimodal_ capacities. While not part of the 2021 set of functionalities, MUM will allow users to use a combination of interfaces to get answers. For instance, multimodal search enables combined searches using image and text. Google’s example is to point the camera at a broken bike component and search “how to fix”, from which MUM would understand the context between the two inputs. In identifying the _intent_ (repair) and the _context_ (camera shows a bicycle’s _derailleur_) Google would know what results to show results from the combination.

![Search on Mobile | GO MO Group](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20700%20700'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

#### How should businesses adapt?

Content marketing is about more than text, even more so after the multimodal search rolls out. Using relevant images and applying proper alt tags will help Google understand your content, and increase the likelihood of your products being shown in multimodal searches.

## Conclusion

Whenever updates to the algorithm are announced (or predicted, for that matter) it is a good idea to think of them in the context of Google’s stated mission for Search: to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful. As such, a constant SEO factor will always be to present the most relevant and useful information for queries relevant to one’s business. CXO and content remain essential to any [B2B digital marketing](https://www.gomogroup.com/insikter/gabriel-ghavami/b2b-digital-marketing/) strategy.

# Harnessing India’s innovation and growth: Insights from Cecilia Oskarsson

In this conversation, **Cecilia Oskarsson,** former Swedish Trade and Invest Commissioner in India, shares her perspective on India’s rapid growth and rising importance as a global investment and innovation hub. From sustainability and manufacturing to talent, infrastructure, and technology, she reflects on why India is uniquely positioned to benefit from major global shifts and what this means for companies looking to expand and grow in one of the world’s most dynamic markets.

### Harnessing India’s innovation and growth

India today represents one of the **most dynamic and fast evolving business environments** in the world. With strong economic momentum, expanding infrastructure, and a rapidly growing talent base, the country is becoming a central hub for innovation, investment, and global collaboration. International companies are increasingly looking at India not just as a market, but as a strategic partner for long term growth, technology development, and sustainable transformation.

> “The pulse, the focus, the energy and the growth that we are seeing in India today is amazing and it’s been fantastic to be able to experience it first row.”

### Understanding the role: Swedish Trade and Invest Commissioner in India

Business Sweden is partly owned by the Swedish government and partly by Swedish businesses. It serves as the Swedish Trade and Invest Council with a clear mission to support cross border growth. The role focuses on helping Swedish companies expand outside Sweden, particularly in markets like India, while also enabling international companies to grow and invest in Sweden. In the India context, the commissioner supports Swedish businesses entering and expanding in the Indian market and encourages Indian companies to explore investment opportunities in Sweden.

### Why India matters right now

India’s investment environment is filled with opportunity for international companies. Strong economic momentum, growing domestic demand, and large scale infrastructure development are driving rapid transformation across industries. The country’s expanding middle class is fuelling consumption and shaping one of the world’s fastest growing markets. At the same time, government investments in infrastructure such as highways and airports are creating new possibilities for global businesses.

#### **Global trends shaping India’s future**

Demographic dividend

India has a growing middle class that is driving consumption and economic growth across sectors.

Deglobalization

Shifts in global supply chains are opening new opportunities for companies to invest and build capabilities in India.

Digitalization

Rapid digital growth is strengthening India’s position as a global technology and innovation hub.

### What this means for growth focused brands

India represents a long term strategic growth market for global companies looking to expand, innovate, and build future ready capabilities. Success in India requires strong local understanding, flexibility, and long term relationship building. Companies that invest early in positioning, partnerships, and innovation are likely to benefit most from the country’s continued growth.

> “Investment environment in India is full of opportunities for international and for Swedish companies.”

### How GO MO Group helps brands grow in evolving markets

As markets like India continue to evolve, brands need stronger visibility, sharper positioning, and data driven strategies to compete and grow. High growth regions demand not only market entry but also sustained digital presence, discoverability, and performance focused marketing that connects with the right audiences.

GO MO Group supports global and B2B brands with strategic insights, digital growth frameworks, and performance marketing solutions that strengthen visibility across search, AI driven platforms, and key digital channels. By combining strategy, technology, and measurable marketing execution, we help brands build relevance, scale faster, and turn market potential into real business growth.

# AI-Driven Revolution: Henrik Anderberg Promoted to CCO

**GOTHENBURG, Sweden – June 20th** – GO MO Group is excited to announce the promotion of [Henrik Anderberg](https://www.gomogroup.com/medarbetare/henrik-anderberg/) to the role of Chief Client Officer (CCO), a crucial position in our transformative journey. Henrik’s extensive industry experience, leadership qualities, and passion for innovation make him the perfect fit to guide us through this significant shift. As CCO, Henrik will play a vital role in ensuring the successful implementation of our strategy and maintaining our commitment to outstanding client impact and satisfaction in this exciting new era. We have full confidence that under his management, GO MO Group will grow, adapt, and excel, consistently surpassing our client’s expectations. Innovation stands as the true defense against irrelevance. This ethos forms the foundation of our significant pivot.

![](https://www.gomogroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/HA-inline.jpg.webp)

[AI transformation](https://www.gomogroup.com/insights/embracing-ai-generated-content-a-strategic-advantage/), shifting B2B buying behaviors, and economic recession forces new paradigms, and GO MO Group must adapt. Generative AI is not only shaking up the game in 2023 – it is drafting an entirely new rulebook.

_“We are undergoing a big transformation, shifting from a generalist [B2B digital marketing](https://www.gomogroup.com/insights/gabriel-ghavami/b2b-sales-as-we-know-it-is-dead/) company to a company lead by self-governing niche marketing agencies, fueled by technology. This shift necessitates severe change management and a fundamental change in habits,”_ says Henrik Anderberg, the newly appointed CCO. _“Each of these agencies are supposed to hold a unique position, tailored to resonate with its specific market sector, in alignment with our steadfast belief that specialists win over generalists in the long run.”_

## Our Leap into Niche Markets: AI as the Accelerator

With the power of cutting-edge AI technologies such as ChatGPT, AmandaAI, and so many others, we are able to leverage advanced tools and platforms that enhance our capabilities, enabling us to craft innovative solutions that not only meet but exceed our clients’ expectations in a sustainable and future-proof manner.

## Embracing a Customer-Centric Ideology: The Core of Our Strategy

Our novel strategy revolves around embracing a truly customer-centric ideology. We delve into the unique needs of each client, delivering segment-based solutions that defy the one-size-fits-all approach. By providing relevant context to groups of companies with shared characteristics, we create tailored strategies that drive impactful results.

## Henrik Anderberg: Guiding the Transformation

_“Henrik Anderberg stands as the embodiment of our bold vision and unwavering commitment to change. With his strong leadership, we have full confidence in our ability to navigate the dynamic marketing landscape and shape the future of our industry. Together, we will fearlessly challenge conventions, redefine the marketing landscape, and deliver exceptional results for our valued clients.”_ – [Gabriel Ghavami](https://www.gomogroup.com/medarbetare/gabriel-ghavami/), Founder and CEO of GO MO Group

![](https://www.gomogroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/Henrik-GO-MO-seminar.jpg.webp)

## Join Us on the Transformative Path

Change is not only essential for growth and progress, but it also presents exciting opportunities on the horizon. We wholeheartedly invite our esteemed clients, valued partners, and industry peers to join us on this transformative journey, where the fusion of human expertise and AI power ignites innovation and paves the way for a future where excellence becomes the new standard.

In conclusion, we humbly embrace the changing landscape and believe our secured future is driven by AI transformation, shifting B2B buying behaviors, and economic recession, as we lead with vision and determination towards a brighter tomorrow.

For further information or media inquiries, please contact: [Timothy Larsson](mailto:timothy@gomogroup.com)

Digital Strategies, Pull marketing, SEO \| READING TIME: 5 MINUTES \| January 22, 2021

# Centralized B2B SEO Facilitates Economies of Scale

How an optimally balanced centralization enables digital economies of scale. What processes should be conducted centrally, and which are more suited for a local implementation? These are some of the topics covered below.

**Global leaders are experts in utilizing advantages from economies of scale within traditional business verticals. Our experience is that the same global leaders, especially B2B companies, are under-leveraging the same skillset when it comes to making use of these advantages in Pull marketing and SEO activities.**

Leaders combine Pull marketing with amazing content to win customers’ attention during their research processes – not always to sell, but to assist in the purchase. The constant search for information on Google has become a vital and determining factor in all purchasing and research processes of the customer buying journey. Meanwhile, [77% of B2B companies](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/insights/b2b-buying-journey) consider their sales processes to be very complex.

Data also shows that 94% of B2B purchases include searching on a search engine like Google. In the wake of the pandemic, and our “New” future, B2B companies have a lot less influence and access to customer relationships. This makes “search” the king of the hill, and one of the prime channels for digital communication. According to data, search results on Google are today considered to be more trustworthy than big brands and traditional media. This data only enhances the fact that companies must work with SEO to build and maintain trust for their brand.

## Utilizing digital economies of scale in SEO

So, how does one make use of scalability and find a good balance of central processes and local activities? **In short, optimal results are gained by applying an 80/20 split. This results in a shared “corporate memory”**, instead of locally constraining business-critical and strategic information.

## 80 centralized, 20 decentralized

A fully decentralized digital marketing strategy and approach is great for small local organizations, and it is often “fun” to work with creative marketing on a local level. However, nine times out of ten, this hurts the overall marketing efforts of a large organization, leading to lower competitive advantage and negative ROI.

An organization whose SEO operations are 80% centralized lets its local teams focus on execution rather than technical SEO and strategy development. While SEO needs to take local phenomena into account and be based on [customers’ local purchasing behavior](https://www.gomogroup.com/en/services/pull-marketing/), only 20% needs to be dedicated to this.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20960%20540'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Increased velocity, better results, and more efficient digital communication

Instead of giving each individual business unit responsibility of finding and curating insights regarding one’s product or service, this process can be centralized, and the information can then be supplied to the local branches. This will create momentum and increased velocity in processes and implementations alike. Our experience is that companies have old processes leaving investments related to IT be centralized. This gives local branches responsibility for marketing and communication in terms of both execution and budget. Companies do this **despite** the fact that digital marketing, and SEO processes in particular, doesn’t need to be managed locally – it doesn’t matter if the report for your latest search engine advertisements’ conversion rate is compiled in Beijing or Malta, the numbers are the same. All this indicates that companies, B2B in particular, have an outdated strategy of centralization. Especially companies with distinct separate business areas or business units.

“…a fortune 500 company who, over a three-year span, through six different persons and four business units, ordered 13 SEO analyses, which ended up showing similar results every time.”

## A slow process that has the organization paying for the same thing several times

Two of the many downsides with having each business unit, region, and/or business area handling “their own” SEO is that the organization (1) experiences negative ROI due to multiple re-investments for the same outcome, and (2) loses momentum, hence they will be unable to move ahead at sufficient speed. Consequently, this process of decentralizing ALL of one’s digital marketing is both expensive and inefficient.

Taking our own experiences as a reference, we have a client, a global leader, and a Fortune 500 company, who, over a three-year span. Through six different marketing managers and four various business units, ordered 13 SEO analyses, which ended up showing similar results every time. Such behavior is akin to 13 people going on a bus trip where everyone rents one bus and a bus driver each, as opposed to sharing one bus.

## The answer: there should be only one captain on the ship, with optimal balance

**Not all analytic activities are to be decentralized.** Instead, a central unit can start the projects and compile general insights and market trends. These can be used to develop local ways of applying the insights or as a foundation for further analyses. **Meaning that the local branches won’t need to start from zero.** The central organization will have already taken the first step, bringing the local teams with them to the next step. After this, it is up to each branch to build upon this and bring themselves to a market leader position. For example: create a [content strategy](https://www.gomogroup.com/en/services/content-marketing-strategy/) centrally, and let the local marketing teams create and implement the content.

## Maximize synergies in centralizing

In centralizing an organization’s analytical operations, it is important to identify what should be performed centrally, and what should be placed closer to production or sales. [The Pareto Principle](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/p/paretoprinciple.asp) also applies in digital marketing, and by centralization of certain parts of the strategic work, local and super local parts of the organization can focus on their most valuable activities.

## One group analysis adds more business value than 13 business unit analyses

Being a marketing agency niched in Pull marketing, we utilize a data-driven approach in our operations, a lot of which involves preparing analyses and creating strategies. We have noticed that it is more efficient to perform one large Pull marketing and SEO analysis compared to several small ones covering the same markets and companies. This means that it is more efficient to do an analysis for a corporate group than to do a standalone analysis for each individual company. There are several reasons for this. First of all, there are general insights for the market, and spillover effects giving the companies in a corporate group similar opportunities. These are more prominent in a large overarching analysis. In addition to this, there are also organizational advantages: instead of each company having its own project manager for the SEO partnership, the project can involve only the agency and a central team.

## Summary

Our recommendation is, as a rule of thumb, to centralize 80% of the marketing budgeting, strategies, and analytics, placing the remaining 20% closer to the local sales teams. Such a distribution lets the organization work optimally towards both overarching and local goals, while also allowing more total resources to be put toward execution.

“Over time, winners keep winning **not** because they have exceptional data and strategy, but because they have systems that enable state-of-the-art execution of strategies.”

We are convinced that speed and execution are key factors for a future-proof digital marketing strategy. Regardless of whether you want to develop a complete digital marketing strategy, or want an in-depth analysis of your market situation, you can utilize our experience of working with market-leading B2B companies.

# Reduce The Bounce

User engagement metrics, what people do when they land on your website, have become an increasingly important factor for organizations trying to engage with their visitors online. [The most important SEO factor](https://www.gomogroup.com/en/insikter/the-top-indicator-of-marketing-performance-increased-sales/) is _Conversion Rate_, how many visitors complete a goal (sales, contact form fills, newsletter signups, etc). However, the conversion rate is dependent on other factors, one of which is the _Bounce Rate_.

Google and other search engines make use of certain metrics that help them gauge whether users are engaging with your site. According to industry expert [Neil Patel](https://neilpatel.com/blog/5-engagement-metrics-thatll-help-improve-your-search-rankings/), these _engagement metrics_ are key to good SEO performance. According to [SEMRush](https://www.semrush.com/ranking-factors/), the bounce rate is the 4th most important ranking factor on SERPs.

Since bounce rate is such an important factor, it is important to know how to improve (decrease) the bounce rate of one’s website. In this article, we will provide tips on how you as an organization can reduce the bounce rate on your website.

However, before we delve deeper into the activities that can reduce the bounce rate of a website, let’s get a better understanding of what exactly the issue is; what does the term ‘bounce rate’ mean?

## Bounce Rate: A Bane For All Marketers

According to [Google](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/1009409?hl=en), a bounce is a single-page session on your site. A bounce is calculated specifically as a session that triggers only a single request to the analytics server, such as when a user opens a single page on your site and then exits without triggering any other requests to the analytics server during that session. In layman terms, the bounce rate of a website is calculated based on the percentage of visitors that leave a webpage without taking any action, such as clicking on a link, filling out a form or making a purchase.

That being said, it is important to define if the bounce rate of your website is high or low, according to your industry standards. [Backlinko](https://backlinko.com/hub/seo/bounce-rate) has provided a breakdown of the average bounce rate for certain online segments. If your website has a higher bounce rate percentage than mentioned for your industry, it is an indicator that you should take actions to improve the bounce rate of your website.

![Average bounce rate](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20720'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Tips To Bounce Back From A High Bounce Rate

### 1\. Be Fast Or Be Last

According to [Pingdom](https://royal.pingdom.com/page-load-time-really-affect-bounce-rate/), there is a clear correlation between page speed and bounce rate. For example, their study reveals that less than 10% of visitors bounce when a page loads within 2 seconds. On the other hand, when the page takes 7 seconds or more to load, over 30% of visitors bounce from your website.

So, if you’re struggling with how to reduce bounce rates, consider speeding up your website. Here are a few easy activities that can help increase your page load speed:

- _Reduce image sizes_
- _Eliminate unnecessary scripts_
- _Deactivate plugins you don’t use_

A popular example of companies benefitting by increasing their page load speed is when [Firefox](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/page-load-time-conversion-rates) reported the number of downloads on their website increased by 15.4% after they reduced the average load time to 2.2 seconds.

### 2\. Content Can Only be King if Readable

It is important to ensure that when a visitor lands on your website, they can read the content without any difficulty. If the user finds it hard to read the content present on your website, they will most likely leave your website and continue browsing other websites.

Consider font size and line height, for instance. A healthy balance between the two characteristics improves readability. You can also improve readability by increasing white space. When you have more white space — also called negative space or blank space — the reader feels less overwhelmed. White space makes the copy scannable.

A great case study of optimizing content to improve bounce rate and eventually conversions is [Forex Trading](https://neilpatel.com/blog/100-conversion-optimization-case-studies/). The company made the content’s font bigger and added more relevant images to their landing page. By simply making these smaller edits to their page, their bounce rate decreased and they noticed a 99.4% increase in conversions.

### 3\. Don’t Confuse Or Lose

If your website is difficult to navigate, the visitor will likely leave your website. Hence, you need to cater to the user’s expectations while creating your website. Instead of focusing too much on creativity, it is recommended to follow best UX practices instead, that will make your website user-friendly and in the long run reduce your bounce rate. For more information on how you can make your website easily accessible for users, we have provides the best UX practices that you should follow while building your website.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201300%20900'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Conclusion

We have compiled this in-depth guide after conducting thorough research, experiments, and analyses of real-life case studies. It is important to understand that tackling the bounce rate of a website depends on not just the type of website and industry, but also the ever-changing Google algorithms. Hence, it is essential to stay up-to-date about the latest trends and techniques to combat high bounce rates.
